claims.text: On 4 September, the US national average retail diesel price passed $5.85 a gallon, breaking the June 2022 record.
And here is the fact that should stop the scroll: crude oil is trading roughly $28 a barrel *cheaper* than it was during the 2022 record.
Aramco's Jazan refinery — 400,000 barrels a day of diesel and gasoline — has not properly run since 27 July, when drones damaged its tank farm and power complex.

**Vector two: the war itself.** At least nine Gulf refineries have been damaged and shut by the fighting, and the region's refining capacity — 11.7 million barrels a day — has no credible restart timeline.
Roughly a third of Russian refining capacity is out — about 5 million barrels a day — and Russian refining has fallen to its lowest level in over two decades.

Russia, historically one of the world's top diesel exporters, collapsed to near-zero diesel exports by late July, extended its diesel export ban through September, banned gasoline exports through January 2027, and is now importing gasoline from Türkiye — the first time ever.

In Kuwait, Iranian drones hit the Mina al-Ahmadi and Mina Abdullah refineries in March — a third strike on al-Ahmadi in early April suspended roughly 346,000 barrels a day of capacity, and Kuwait's crude exports briefly hit zero.
Israel's Haifa refinery — 197,000 barrels a day, two-thirds of the country's processing — took Iranian missile hits in March and June;

Libya's Zawiya refinery, the country's largest at 120,000 barrels a day, absorbed a week of unclaimed drone strikes in August — naphtha tank, petrol tank, blending plant — forcing force-majeure warnings.

Both arrive against buffers that no longer exist: US distillate stocks are the lowest for early September since 1982, and on the East Coast — the region that heats with oil — inventories hit 19.3 million barrels in late August, the lowest in records going back to 1990.
The EIA expects national stocks to fall below 100 million barrels this month, first time since 2003, and to stay below the five-year average for most of 2027.
Canadian crude arriving at the US Gulf Coast fell from about 526,000 barrels a day in 2024 to roughly 337,000 in the first half of this year.
